t: Find Latest Group of Size M - Incremental Run-Length Tracking
o: Bits flip from 0 to 1 one position per step, and after each step the string decomposes into maximal runs (groups) of consecutive ones. We must remember the most recent step at which some run had length exactly m. The crucial observation is locality: lighting position p can only change three run lengths - the run ending at p-1, the run starting at p+1, and their merger of length L + R + 1. Keeping a histogram of current run lengths therefore lets us ask "does a run of length m exist?" in O(1) after every activation. In Example 1, step 4 merges positions 1-2 with the isolated 1 at position... more precisely it grows 0101 into 11101, leaving runs 3 and 1, so m = 1 still exists and the answer is 4; by step 5 the sole run has length 5 and no size-m run remains.
k: Activating position p only alters three lengths: the left run L, the right run R, and the merged run L + R + 1.
Store each run length at both boundary cells so any future merge discovers it in O(1).
Maintain cnt[len] = number of live runs of each length; cnt[m] greater than 0 after step i records ans = i - and never stop early, since later merges can destroy all size-m runs.

a.n: Approach 1: Full Rescan After Each Step
a.i: Simulate the process literally: keep the bit array, and after every activation rescan all n cells tallying maximal run lengths to see whether length m exists anywhere. This transparently matches the problem statement and is impossible to overcomplicate, but the per-step scan makes it O(n^2) overall - acceptable for tiny inputs, hopeless at n = 10^5. Use it to frame the discussion, then improve it.
s: Maintain a boolean array of the n bits.
After setting bit arr[i] = 1, scan the entire array left to right.
Track the current run length; mark the step as good if any run hits exactly m.
Keep the last good step as the answer, or -1 if none.
a.t: O(n^2) - one full-array scan for each of the n activations.

a.n: Approach 2: Boundary Lengths with a Length Histogram
a.i: Store len[i] = length of the run containing activated cell i, stamped at both ends of the run. When p lights up, read L = len[p-1] and R = len[p+1]; the merged run has length L + R + 1, so write that value at cells p-L and p+R, the two boundaries. In parallel maintain cnt[x] = how many live runs have length x: decrement for L and R when nonzero, increment for the merged length. Whenever cnt[m] is positive after step i, record ans = i and continue to the end so the latest qualifying step wins.
s: Zero-initialize len[], then process activations arr[1..n] in order.
Read neighbor run lengths L = len[p-1] and R = len[p+1].
Stamp cur = L + R + 1 at len[p-L] and len[p+R].
Update cnt: remove L and R (if nonzero), add cur.
Set ans = i whenever cnt[m] exceeds zero; return ans or -1.
a.t: O(n) - a fixed handful of array updates per activation.
a.sp: O(n) - the len and cnt arrays.

a.n: Approach 3: Union-Find with a Size Histogram
a.i: Model runs as disjoint-set components: activating p creates a singleton and unions with whichever neighbors are already active, so components always coincide with current runs. Track component sizes and a histogram over them; a union removes the two absorbed sizes from the histogram and adds the combined size. Exactly as before, the answer is the latest step whose histogram shows at least one component of size m. Same asymptotic cost as boundary arrays, but the DSU framing extends naturally to richer connectivity questions.
s: Activate p with tentative size 1; for each active neighbor, fold its root size in and attach that root under p.
Update the size histogram: subtract absorbed sizes, add the merged size.
Record ans = step whenever a size-m component exists.
Return ans (or -1) after processing the permutation.
a.t: O(n * alpha(n)) - near-linear inverse-Ackermann union-find work overall.
a.sp: O(n) - parent, size, and histogram arrays.

w: Explain the histogram idea, then implement the boundary-length method - it is the shortest optimal code and needs no data structures beyond two arrays; mention DSU as the alternative when connectivity questions multiply. The biggest trap is stopping at the first step with a size-m run: later merges can eliminate every such run (Example 2 returns -1), so track the answer across all steps. Others: forgetting to stamp the merged length at BOTH boundaries, or updating the histogram before capturing the old neighbor sizes. Follow-ups: answer for several m values at once (keep the full histogram and query it), or support toggling bits off, where plain DSU struggles and ordered sets over run boundaries shine.
